theme: The golden calf; Moses intercedes; God’s glory and grace
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 32:1-33:23. This is one of the most dramatic passages in the Bible. The people break the covenant within weeks of making it, and Moses pleads for them on the mountain. Read it slowly and notice who speaks, who changes, and who is revealed.
settingTheScene: Moses has been on the mountain for forty days, and the people below have grown restless. They believe he will not come back. While God is giving instructions for a house where he will live, Israel is building an idol at the foot of the mountain. The golden calf is the most serious sin of Israel in the wilderness, and its effects run through the rest of the Old Testament. It is also the occasion for one of the most powerful scenes of intercession in all of Scripture.
observation: The people say, “Up, make us gods who shall go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him” (32:1).
Aaron collects gold, forms a calf, and declares a feast to the LORD (32:2-6). They say, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (32:4).
God tells Moses, “Your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves” (32:7).

Moses pleads with God, appealing to his reputation and to his promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Israel (32:11-13). “And the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people” (32:14).
Moses breaks the tablets, grinds up the calf, and makes the people drink it (32:19-20).
The Levites rally to Moses, and about three thousand die (32:26-28).
Moses says, “Now, if you will forgive their sin, but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written” (32:32).
God promises, “My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest” (33:14). Moses asks, “Please show me your glory” (33:18).
interpretation:
The golden calf is a lesson in how quickly people fall. Israel has just heard God speak, and they have promised, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do” (24:7). Within weeks, they are worshiping an idol. The sin is not that they stopped worshiping the LORD. They called the calf their deliverer from Egypt and held a feast “to the LORD.” Their sin was to make God into what they wanted him to be, a visible and manageable image. The second commandment was broken before the ink was dry.

Notice what God says to Moses. “Your people, whom you brought up.” God speaks as if Israel were no longer his. Moses answers by saying, “Your people, whom you have brought out.” It is a quiet but important exchange. Moses will not let go of the relationship. He argues from God’s own words and God’s own name. It is a model of prayer: Moses holds God to his promises, and God relents.

Moses’ offer in 32:32 is stunning. He asks to be blotted out of God’s book if the people cannot be forgiven. He is willing to bear their punishment. God does not accept the offer. No ordinary man can pay for another man’s sin. But the offer points ahead to someone who can.

Chapter 33 is the heart of the passage. God says that he will send an angel but will not go with them, because they are a “stiff-necked people.” Moses will not move without the presence of God. “If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here” (33:15). The whole point of the exodus was to bring God’s presence among them. Without it, the land would mean nothing. God agrees. Then Moses asks for the most daring thing: “Please show me your glory.” God answers by showing his goodness and proclaiming his name, and he covers Moses in the cleft of the rock, so that Moses sees only God’s back. No sinner can see God’s face and live.
connection: Paul says that Christ has done what Moses offered but could not do: he became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and he was “made sin” on our behalf (2 Corinthians 5:21). Paul also wished himself accursed for his people (Romans 9:3), echoing Moses. Jesus, the “one mediator between God and men” (1 Timothy 2:5), intercedes for us (Hebrews 7:25). John says that no one has ever seen God, but the Son “has made him known” (John 1:18). Paul says that we see the glory of God “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).
application:
Ask what idol you are tempted to build when God seems to be slow. Name it honestly in prayer.

Learn from Moses’ example. Use God’s own promises when you pray. Find one promise in this week’s reading and pray it back to him.

Echo Moses’ words: “If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here.” Ask God to make his presence the thing you want most.
prayerPrompts: Confess the idols you make when you are impatient.
Thank Jesus for doing what Moses could not.
Ask him to go with you, and to make his presence more precious than anything else.
